definition: A worker that runs one piece of code at a time; your program always starts with one, the main thread.
A running program with its own private memory; threads live inside a process.
A team of on-call workers .NET keeps ready so you can hand in tasks without creating threads yourself.
A promise that some work will finish later; a Task represents it in C#.
A keyword that marks a method as able to pause at an await and resume later.
A keyword that means: pause here until the task is done, without blocking a thread — like sitting down until your coffee buzzer goes off.
A single bathroom key for a piece of code: only one thread can be inside the locked block at a time.
A parking lot with a fixed number of spaces; when it is full, arriving threads wait for a free spot.
A bug where the result depends on which thread happens to run first, so it can change from run to run.
Two or more threads each waiting for something the other holds, so nobody can ever move again.
An operation that happens completely or not at all — no other thread can see it half-done.
A keyword telling the compiler and CPU to always read the latest value of a field, never a cached copy.
A polite 'please stop' signal you pass into work so it can shut down cleanly when asked.
When the CPU pauses one thread and resumes another — like a chef swapping between dishes.
Concurrent means many tasks in progress at once (like one chef juggling dishes); parallel means truly running at the same instant on multiple cores.
A helper that decides which thread an awaited method resumes on — for example, back on the UI thread in a desktop app.
Making a thread sit and wait doing nothing, like standing at the door until a delivery arrives.
When a thread never gets a turn to run because other threads always win the competition.
Threads that keep reacting to each other and stay busy but make no progress — like two people sidestepping in a corridor forever.
A meeting point where several threads wait until everyone has arrived, then all continue together.
